title: The Interplay of Data Structure and Imbalance in the Learning Dynamics of Diffusion Models
claim: Under weak imbalance both classes transition together, but strong imbalance splits their transition times, delaying the minority class.
layout: 4 panels in a row, shared x-axis, dashed theory over solid simulations
description: A single row of four small line plots with a shared x-axis, rescaled time t/log(N). The y-axis is RMS overlap, running from 1 to 0. A legend at top left marks Class 1 as blue and Class 2 as red. The first panel is titled 'Weak imbalance'. The other three sit under a 'Strong imbalance' header and are labeled a = 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4. Solid curves go from light to dark to show growing system size, and they drop from 1 to near 0 like sigmoids. Dashed step functions show the asymptotic theory, black in the weak panel and blue or red in the strong panels. In the weak panel both classes drop at about the same time, around 0.45 to 0.5. In the strong panels the red class drops earlier than the blue, so the two classes separate. The eye goes first to the sharp drops and the gap between red and blue.
caption: Strong imbalance induces separation in inference times. Root mean square (RMS) overlaps between the projected centroids $\bm{\mu}_c$ (Eq. [ref]) and the top principal components ($\bm{\psi}_{1},\bm{\psi}_{2}$) of $U_{\mathrm{gep}}$, defined as $\operatorname{RMS}_c\equiv \operatorname{Mean}(\sum_{i=1}^2(\bm{\mu}_c\cdot \bm{\psi}_i)^2/\lVert \bm{\mu}_c \lVert^2)^{1/2}$, as a function of rescaled diffusion time $\widetilde{t}\equiv t/\log N$. Left panel corresponds to weak imbalance ($b_1=0.7, b_2=0.3$, Eq. [ref]), while the remaining panels illustrate instances of strong imbalance ($b_1=1-N^{-a}$, $b_2=N^{-a}$, Eq. [ref]). Dashed lines denote asymptotic theoretical predictions from Eqs.[ref],[ref]; continuous lines represent finite-size numerical simulations for $N \in \{50, 500, 5000\}$ and $P \in \{100, 1000, 10000\}$, with increasing system size indicated by darker colors. Simulations show convergence toward the predicted asymptotic limits. Parameter values: $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=0.5$, $\lVert \bm{m}_1 \lVert= \lVert \bm{m}_2 \lVert = \sqrt{N}$, $\bm{m}_1\cdot \bm{m}_2=0$, $M=2000$, $N_{runs}=50$ for $P=100, 1000$ and $N_{runs}=10$ for $P=10000$.
abstract: Real-world datasets are inherently heterogeneous, yet how per-class structural differences and sampling imbalance shape the training dynamics of diffusion models---and potentially exacerbate disparities---remains poorly understood. While models typically transition from an initial phase of generalization to memorizing the training set, existing theory assumes homogeneous data, leaving open how class imbalance and heterogeneity reshape these dynamics. In this work, we develop a high-dimensional analytical framework to study class-dependent learning in score-based diffusion models. Analyzing a random-features model trained on Gaussian mixtures, we derive the feature-covariance spectrum to characterize per-class generalization and memorization times. We reveal the explicit hierarchy governing these dynamics: class variance is the primary determinant of learning order---consistently favoring higher-variance classes---while centroid geometry and sampling imbalance play secondary roles. Specifically, sampling imbalance acts as a modulator that can reverse this ordering and, under strong imbalance, forces minority classes to acquire distinct, delayed inference times during backward diffusion. Together, these results suggest that diffusion models can memorize some classes while others remain insufficiently learned. We validate our theoretical predictions empirically using U-Net models trained on Fashion MNIST.
